title: URL Encode and Decode — Handle Special Characters Correctly

content.intro: URLs can only contain a limited set of ASCII characters. Special characters, spaces and non-Latin scripts must be percent-encoded. The URL Encode/Decode tool does this automatically — paste your text, get a safe URL, or paste an encoded string and get the readable version back.

sections.heading: What is Percent Encoding?
sections.body: Percent encoding replaces unsafe characters with a percent sign followed by two hexadecimal digits. A space becomes %20, @ becomes %40, and Chinese characters such as 你好 become %E4%BD%A0%E5%A5%BD. RFC 3986 defines which characters must be encoded and where.

sections.heading: Reserved vs Unreserved Characters
sections.body: Reserved characters have structural meaning in a URL: : / ? # [ ] @ ! $ & ' ( ) * + , ; = . They should be encoded when they are used as data rather than as URL structure. Unreserved characters (A-Z, a-z, 0-9, -, _, ., ~) are always safe and are left untouched.

sections.heading: encodeURI vs encodeURIComponent
sections.body: JavaScript's encodeURI() preserves URL structure characters such as ? & and #. encodeURIComponent() encodes everything, which is what you want for a query parameter value. Example: encodeURIComponent('name=John&age=30') returns 'name%3DJohn%26age%3D30'. Using the wrong one leaves dangerous characters unencoded or breaks the parameter.

sections.heading: Common URL Encoding Mistakes
sections.body: Double encoding: encoding an already-encoded string produces garbled URLs such as %2520 instead of %20. Missing encoding: unencoded spaces break URLs in most contexts. Wrong function: encodeURI on a query parameter value can leave reserved characters that change the meaning of the URL.

content.conclusion: URL encoding is fundamental to web development. Whether you're building query strings, form submissions, or API calls, Craftisle's encoder ensures your URLs are always valid and safe.
